overview: This domain is about making sure every person and system that touches an organization's data is known, proven and limited to what it needs. Topic 3.1 follows an identity from creation, through job changes and reviews, to removal, and covers how people, systems and outside users prove who they are. Topic 3.2 covers the rules that limit what an identity can do: least privilege, separation of duties and the access control models. As an entry-level practitioner, you run these processes, notice when they break and raise gaps with the right owner.
analogy: Think of a hotel. The front desk checks a guest's ID before handing over a key card, and the card opens only that guest's room and the gym. Staff cards open more doors, but the master card is kept in the safe and signed out. When a guest changes rooms, the old card stops working; at checkout it is canceled. The delivery robot gets its own card that opens only the service lift, and each night someone checks which cards are still active.

topics.overview: The identity life cycle is the path every account follows: a role is defined, the account is created with approved access, access changes and is checked as duties change, and the account is removed when no longer needed. This topic also covers how people and systems prove who they are, sessions, outside users, and the frameworks and tools that run the cycle.
can_do: Put joiner, mover and leaver tasks in the right order, including removing old access when someone changes jobs
Tell true multifactor authentication from two checks of the same factor, and name phishing-resistant options
Explain what an access review checks, who signs it off and what happens to access nobody confirms
Manage service accounts, bots, AI agents and outside users through the same life cycle as staff

subtopics.name: Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle
subtopics.definition: An identity represents one person or system; accounts are its logins on specific systems. The identity life cycle manages both, from creation to removal.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Access can only be controlled and traced when every account belongs to a known identity with an owner. Orphaned and shared accounts give attackers easy doors.
how_it_works: Identification is the claim, such as a username; authentication proves it; authorization sets what it may do.
Each person or system, AI agents included, gets one unique identity, so every logged action traces back to the right actor.
Joiner, mover and leaver stages create, adjust and remove access, while reviews run alongside.
A trusted record, usually from human resources (HR), triggers each stage.

types.meaning: Everyday access for one named person
Administrator rights that can change systems, security settings or other users' access
Used by an application or process, not a person (see 3.1.12)
One login for several people; it hides who acted, so avoid it
Short-term access for an outsider or a project, with an end date (see 3.1.15)

subtopics.example: At a bus company, an HR start record creates an account for Sam, a new dispatcher. When Sam moves to payroll, the dispatch rights go; when Sam leaves, the account is disabled that day. Each month Lee, a junior analyst, matches accounts to HR records and logs any ownerless account in the access team's queue.

review: Match the active account list against current HR records
Confirm every shared or service account has a named owner
evidence: Directory export showing each account's owner and last sign-in
HR joiner, mover and leaver reports for the same period
audit_focus.recommend: Report ownerless accounts to the access management team and system owner; do not delete them yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner keeps or removes an unowned account

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every account needs one identity, one accountable owner and a trusted trigger for each stage. Report any account nobody can explain.

exam_traps.trap: Typing a username proves who someone is.
exam_traps.why: A username is only a claim. Proof comes from authentication, such as a password plus a second factor.

exam_traps.trap: A shared team login is fine when everyone needs the same access.
exam_traps.why: Shared logins hide who did what. Give each person their own account with the same role.

key_terms.definition: An active account whose owner has left or cannot be found.
The three events that trigger access changes: starting, changing jobs and leaving.

subtopics.memory_aid: Claim, prove, permit: identification, authentication, authorization.

subtopics.name: Defining Roles and Entitlements
subtopics.definition: Defining roles means grouping the access a job needs into a named role, so people get a standard, approved set of entitlements instead of one-off grants.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Clear roles make provisioning consistent and reviews possible. Without them, access is copied from coworkers and people collect rights they never needed.
how_it_works: List the job's tasks, then the systems and permissions each task needs.
The business or data owner approves the role's contents; IT builds it.
Check each role for separation of duties conflicts before approval (see 3.2.3).
Meet one person's extra need with a time-limited request, not a wider role.
subtopics.example: A city library defines a circulation clerk role: check items in and out and view borrower details, but not waive fines. When a supervisor asks to let one clerk waive fines for a week, Priya, a junior access administrator, opens a temporary request with an end date for the branch manager to approve.

review: Trace each permission in a role to a task
Confirm one-off grants have approval and an end date
evidence: Role catalog listing each role, its permissions and its owner
Approval records showing who signed off each role change
audit_focus.recommend: Raise roles that mix conflicting duties with the role owner before anyone is assigned them.
audit_focus.decides: The business or data owner signs off each role and later changes to it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Roles come from duties, not a coworker's access. The data owner approves; IT builds. An unusual need gets a time-limited exception.

exam_traps.trap: Copy a coworker's access for a new hire on the same team.
exam_traps.why: The coworker may hold leftover rights from past jobs. The approved role gives only what the job needs.

exam_traps.trap: IT should decide what each role contains, because IT runs the systems.
exam_traps.why: IT builds roles, but the business or data owner knows the work and is accountable for approving it.

key_terms.definition: A single permission, such as reading a folder or approving payments.
So many narrow or custom roles that nobody can manage or review them.

subtopics.name: Provisioning and Identity Proofing
subtopics.definition: Provisioning creates an account and grants its approved access. Identity proofing first checks that the person is who they claim to be, before credentials are issued.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Getting access right on day one is easier than fixing it later. Weak proofing lets an impostor be enrolled with legitimate credentials.
how_it_works: Requests come from a trusted source, such as a human resources (HR) start record, not a chat message.
Accounts prepared before a start date stay disabled until the person's first day.
The manager or data owner approves; the approver should not also build the account.
Proofing checks evidence, such as photo ID, more strictly for riskier access.
First credentials go to a channel on file and are changed at first sign-in.
subtopics.example: A logistics firm hires a remote coordinator, Jordan. On a video call, Mei, the help desk technician, compares Jordan's photo ID with the HR file. When Jordan asks for the setup link at a personal email address, Mei pauses, checks the onboarding procedure and sends it to the work phone on file.

review: Match each new account to an HR record
Compare granted access with the approved role
evidence: The access request ticket with the owner's approval
Provisioning log showing who created the account and when
audit_focus.recommend: Send urgent requests with no HR record to your supervisor or the access management team.
audit_focus.decides: The hiring manager signs off a newcomer's starting access

subtopics.isaca_rule: No record, no account. Prove the person, start with the smallest fitting role and send credentials only to a channel on file.

exam_traps.trap: An urgent request from a senior manager justifies skipping approval.
exam_traps.why: Urgency and authority are classic social engineering pressure. Follow the process; a real manager can approve properly.

exam_traps.trap: Give new staff broad access first and trim it later.
exam_traps.why: Later rarely comes, and the extra access is live from day one.

key_terms.definition: How strongly an identity was checked at enrollment; the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines three levels.
Linking a verified person to their first authenticators.

subtopics.name: Authentication Factors and MFA
subtopics.definition: Authentication factors are categories of proof: something you know, something you have and something you are. Multifactor authentication (MFA) combines at least two different categories.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Stolen passwords are common. A second factor from a different category means an attacker must steal two unlike things.
how_it_works: Count categories, not steps: a password plus a PIN or security question is still one factor.
Two-step verification is MFA only when the steps use different categories.
Biometric readers can accept an impostor or reject a real user, and a copied trait cannot be changed.
Tightening a reader's match threshold cuts false acceptances but raises false rejections; loosening it does the reverse.
Authenticators have a life cycle: enroll after proofing, revoke lost ones, enroll replacements.

types.meaning: A secret held in memory: password, passphrase or PIN
An object you hold: a phone with an authenticator app, a security key or a smart card
A body trait: fingerprint, face, iris or voice

subtopics.example: Alex, a dental hygienist, loses the phone holding their authenticator app and asks for password-only sign-in 'just for today'. Following the lost-device procedure, Sam, the IT assistant, verifies Alex with the practice manager by a known number, removes the lost phone from the account and enrolls a new authenticator.

review: Name each sign-in step's category before calling it MFA
Confirm lost or replaced authenticators are removed from accounts
evidence: Authentication standard listing the methods each group must use
Sign-in logs showing which method each user actually used
audit_focus.recommend: Report systems that accept a password alone for remote or administrator access to the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner applies the methods the authentication standard requires

subtopics.isaca_rule: MFA means two different categories of know, have and are. When an authenticator is lost, verify and replace it; never drop to one factor.

exam_traps.trap: A password and a PIN together count as MFA.
exam_traps.why: Both are things you know. MFA needs another category, such as a phone app (have) or a fingerprint (are).

exam_traps.trap: A user who loses their phone can sign in with a password alone until a new one arrives.
exam_traps.why: That switches MFA off just when an attacker may hold the device. Verify, revoke and re-enroll instead.

key_terms.definition: How often a biometric reader lets in an impostor; the security failure.
How often a biometric reader turns away the real user; the convenience failure.
Where false acceptance and false rejection rates are equal; lower means a more accurate reader, and moving the threshold does not change it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Know, have, are: pick two different ones.

subtopics.name: Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys
subtopics.definition: Phishing-resistant authentication ties each sign-in to the genuine site, so a fake site cannot capture and reuse it. Passkeys and Fast Identity Online 2 (FIDO2) security keys are examples.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Codes from multifactor authentication (MFA) can be relayed through fake login pages, and push prompts repeated until a tired user approves.
how_it_works: A passkey's private key is never sent to any site, nor is the PIN or fingerprint that unlocks it; it signs a challenge only for the real site.
The browser checks the site's address, so a look-alike domain gets nothing it can reuse.
Text and app codes can be typed into a fake page and relayed to the real site at once.
Number matching stops blind approvals, but a fake page can show the real number, so it is not phishing-resistant.
Synced passkeys copy across a user's devices; device-bound security keys never leave one.
Offering a weaker option beside passkeys, such as a texted code, lets a fake page ask for that instead.

rows.label: Factor category
cells: Have (the phone number)
Have (the phone app)
Have, usually unlocked by a PIN or fingerprint

rows.label: Stops a fake login page?
cells: No; the code can be relayed
No; a tired user may approve
Yes; it works only on the real site

rows.label: Main weakness
cells: Subscriber identity module (SIM) swap: the number is moved to an attacker's phone
Repeated prompts until someone taps approve
A lost device needs a tested recovery method

subtopics.example: Ravi, a credit union teller, gets five sign-in prompts at 2 a.m. without trying to log in. Half asleep, Ravi almost taps approve, but denies each one and reports it to the security team at once, so the team can reset the stolen password.

review: Look for bursts of prompts users did not start
Confirm administrators use passkeys or security keys, not text codes
evidence: Alerts for repeated denied or unexpected push prompts
Authenticator report showing each user's methods and backups
audit_focus.recommend: Report unexpected MFA prompts to the security team at once; the password is probably known.
audit_focus.decides: The security manager sets, in the authentication standard, which MFA methods each group uses

subtopics.isaca_rule: Not all MFA is equal. For administrators and other high-risk users, prefer site-bound methods such as passkeys, which a fake page cannot reuse.

exam_traps.trap: Any MFA stops phishing.
exam_traps.why: Codes and push approvals can be relayed or approved by a tired user. Only site-bound methods resist that relay.

exam_traps.trap: An unexpected MFA prompt is just a glitch.
exam_traps.why: A prompt you did not start usually means someone has your password. Deny it and report it.

key_terms.definition: An open standard for signing in with a key pair instead of a shared secret; passkeys use it.
Sending push prompts again and again until the user approves one to make them stop.
The user types a number shown on the login screen, so a blind approval fails.

subtopics.name: Passwords and Modern Password Standards
subtopics.definition: A password standard sets the rules for creating, checking and storing passwords. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) favors length and breach screening over character mixes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Old rules pushed people toward patterns like Summer2026! and sticky notes. The policy says passwords must be strong; the standard sets the exact numbers.
how_it_works: At least 15 characters when a password is the only factor, and 8 alongside another factor.
Allow at least 64 characters and pasting, so password managers work (habits: see 2.3.6).
Screen new passwords against a blocklist; do not demand character mixes or scheduled changes.
Force a change on evidence of compromise, limit failed attempts and store only salted hashes from a slow, password-specific algorithm; a fast hash such as SHA-256 is cracked quickly.
subtopics.example: At a ski resort, Marta, a lift supervisor, resets their password to one they also used on a shopping site that was breached. The new screening check refuses it, and Marta phones IT to ask for an exception. Joel, the IT assistant, explains the blocklist, keeps the check in place and helps Marta create a long passphrase in the password manager.

review: Compare live directory settings with each rule in the standard
Check breach-screening alerts for passwords the security team must reset
evidence: Directory password settings for length, lockout and expiry
Breached-password screening results for newly set passwords
audit_focus.recommend: Send suggested changes to the owner of the password standard; do not change live password settings yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The security manager approves the password standard, within policy senior management approved

subtopics.isaca_rule: Length beats complexity, and screening beats expiry: change a password because of a breach, not the calendar.

exam_traps.trap: Store passwords encrypted so the help desk can recover forgotten ones.
exam_traps.why: Anything that can be decrypted can be stolen and read. Store salted, slow hashes; reset through verified recovery.

exam_traps.trap: Security questions are a safe way to let users reset their own passwords.
exam_traps.why: Answers are often public or guessable, and NIST's guidelines say not to use them. Use another authenticator.

key_terms.definition: A password hash made with a random value added first, so identical passwords give different results; use a slow hashing algorithm.
Slowing or locking sign-in after failed attempts, so guessing takes too long.
Common, expected and breached passwords that new passwords are checked against.
Converting data into another format, such as Base64, so systems can handle it; anyone can reverse it without a key, so it is not encryption.

subtopics.name: Single Sign-On and Federation
subtopics.definition: Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user sign in once at an identity provider and reach many applications; federation extends that trust to applications run by other organizations.
subtopics.why_it_matters: SSO means fewer passwords and one off switch, but it concentrates risk: one stolen login or outage affects every app.
how_it_works: The identity provider checks the user and vouches to the app, which never sees the password.
Strong multifactor authentication (MFA) at the identity provider protects every connected app.
Federation lets a partner's or cloud provider's app accept your sign-ins (see 3.1.15).
Disabling a user stops new sign-ins, but open sessions may last until revoked.

rows.label: Main job
cells: Web sign-on, often for business applications
Sign-on for web and mobile apps
Lets an app reach data on a user's behalf

rows.label: Proves who the user is?
cells: Yes
Yes; it adds identity to OAuth 2.0
No; it grants limited access, not identity

rows.label: What it sends
cells: A signed note saying who you are
A signed ID card plus a pass to reach data
Only a limited pass to reach data, no proof of who you are

subtopics.example: A recycling company signs staff in to email, the route planner and the weighbridge app through SSO. When Owen, a dispatcher, leaves, Lina, the help desk technician, disables Owen's account at the identity provider as the leaver checklist directs. Next morning the route planner shows Owen still signed in on a depot tablet, so Lina ends that session and notes it on the ticket.

review: Confirm the identity provider enforces MFA for every user
Confirm application sessions end when an account is disabled
evidence: Identity provider sign-in logs for failed and unusual sign-ins
Applications that still allow a local password beside SSO
audit_focus.recommend: Report applications with local logins that bypass SSO to the system owner.
audit_focus.decides: System owners and the security team decide which apps use SSO

subtopics.isaca_rule: Guard the identity provider hardest, with strong MFA and monitoring. Disabling the account starts removal; ending sessions finishes it.

exam_traps.trap: SSO is less secure because one password opens everything.
exam_traps.why: SSO concentrates risk, but with strong MFA it usually beats many reused passwords. Protect the identity provider.

exam_traps.trap: OAuth 2.0 proves who the user is.
exam_traps.why: OAuth 2.0 grants an app limited access. Proof of identity comes from OpenID Connect, built on top of it.

key_terms.definition: The trusted service that authenticates users and vouches for them to apps.
The app that accepts the identity provider's statement; also called a service provider.

subtopics.name: Adaptive Authentication and AI Behavior Analysis
subtopics.definition: Adaptive, or risk-based, authentication adjusts sign-in checks to the risk of each attempt, often using AI models that learn each user's normal behavior and flag unusual activity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fixed rules miss stolen credentials used normally. Behavior analysis can catch an attacker who has the right password.
how_it_works: Each sign-in is scored on signals such as device, location, time and usage patterns.
Low risk passes, medium risk asks for a stronger factor, and high risk is blocked for review.
Models err both ways and drift, so people review alerts and tune thresholds.
Behavior data is personal data: collect only what is needed and tell users.
subtopics.example: A hospital's sign-in system flags Dana, a nurse, signing in from abroad minutes after badging into the ward, and demands a security key. Kim, a security operations analyst, confirms Dana is on shift, opens an incident ticket as the playbook directs and calls the incident response lead, who has the password reset.

review: Compare each high-risk alert with facts, such as shift rotas
Confirm alerts that proved false are recorded for tuning
evidence: Risk-scored sign-in events with the signals behind each score
History of alerts marked true or false positive
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate a confirmed account takeover to the incident response lead, not just a password reset.
audit_focus.decides: The security manager approves risk thresholds and what each level triggers

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI scoring adds a layer; it never replaces strong factors or human judgment.

exam_traps.trap: With AI behavior analysis running, a second factor is no longer needed.
exam_traps.why: Scoring decides when to ask for more proof; it still needs strong factors to ask for.

exam_traps.trap: Every AI risk alert means the account is compromised.
exam_traps.why: Travel and new devices cause false alarms. Check each alert against facts, such as the person's schedule.

key_terms.definition: Tools that learn normal behavior for users, devices and accounts and flag unusual activity.
Asking for a stronger or extra factor only when a sign-in or action looks risky.

subtopics.name: Movers and Privilege Creep
subtopics.definition: A mover is a person whose job or duties change. Handling a mover adds the new role's access and removes old access the new role does not need.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Movers are the stage most often missed. Keeping old rights at each move builds privilege creep and can create separation of duties conflicts.
how_it_works: A human resources (HR) transfer record triggers the mover process.
Remove old access at the move, not at the next review.
Check combined old and new rights for conflicts, such as raising and approving one payment.
The new manager approves new access; the old manager confirms what can go.
subtopics.example: At a furniture maker, Bo has moved from sales to design to logistics in four years. The yearly access review shows Bo still holds rights from all three jobs. Kemi, a junior access analyst, asks each system's owner to confirm which old rights can go, then logs a problem ticket because the mover process missed every transfer.

review: Review each mover's rights after the job change
Look for handover access still active past its end date
evidence: HR transfer records matched to access changes in the directory
Users holding rights from more than one role
audit_focus.recommend: Raise conflicting old and new rights with the data owner before the move completes.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides whether old access may stay, and how long

subtopics.isaca_rule: A transfer is a leaver plus a joiner: remove the old access, then add the new.

exam_traps.trap: Movers keep old access in case their old team needs help.
exam_traps.why: That builds privilege creep. Handover access, if truly needed, is approved separately and expires.

exam_traps.trap: The next access review will catch leftover mover access.
exam_traps.why: Reviews are a backstop, often months apart. Removing access at the move closes the gap the day it opens.

key_terms.definition: The buildup of unneeded access as people change jobs and keep old rights.
Old-role access kept briefly, with approval and an end date, to pass work on.

subtopics.name: Access Reviews and Recertification
subtopics.definition: An access review is a regular check, by someone who knows the work, that each account and right is still needed. Recertification is the formal sign-off of that check.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Gaps happen: a missed mover, an emergency grant never removed, a forgotten test account. Reviews catch what slipped through.
how_it_works: The reviewer is the manager or data owner, never the person whose access is reviewed.
Reviews run on a schedule, more often for privileged and sensitive access.
Each right is confirmed or removed; access nobody confirms is removed.
Usage reports can inform a review, but they show what is used, not what is needed; the owner still decides.
The review ends when removals are done in the systems, not when the form is signed.

types.meaning: A manager confirms the access of each person on their team
A system or data owner confirms who may reach their asset
A review triggered by a job change, incident or reorganization rather than the calendar

subtopics.example: Dr. Okafor, owner of a university research database, approves all 300 accounts on the quarterly review in four minutes. Riley, the junior analyst running it, notices and finds 20 accounts of graduated students. Riley sends those back for a decision on each, then tracks the removals until the system shows them gone.

review: Confirm each review line reached the accountable owner
Confirm each removal decision shows as done in the system
evidence: Review sign-offs with the time each reviewer spent
Before-and-after account lists proving removals happened
audit_focus.recommend: Report overdue or rubber-stamped reviews to the review owner's manager or the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The data or system owner certifies who keeps access

subtopics.isaca_rule: A review counts only when the right person decides every line and the removals happen. Unconfirmed access is removed.

exam_traps.trap: Users should review their own access, since they know what they use.
exam_traps.why: That is a conflict of interest. The accountable manager or data owner confirms access.

exam_traps.trap: The review is complete once the owner signs it.
exam_traps.why: Signing is only the decision. It is complete when every removal is done and visible.

key_terms.definition: Approving every line of a review without really checking it.
An account unused for a set period; Center for Internet Security (CIS) guidance suggests disabling it after 45 days.

subtopics.name: Deprovisioning Leavers
subtopics.definition: Deprovisioning removes an identity's access when it is no longer needed: disabling accounts, revoking credentials and sessions, and collecting devices and badges.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Accounts left behind by former staff, contractors and vendors are a common route for misuse. Prompt removal also protects former staff from blame.
how_it_works: The human resources (HR) exit record triggers removal; for a hostile exit, access is cut as the person is told.
Disable first and delete later under the retention policy, so logs stay traceable.
Revoke more than the password: sessions, tokens and remote access.
Have shared secrets changed, collect devices and badges, and reassign the person's data.
subtopics.example: Dev, an account manager at a freight broker, retires on Friday. Following the leaver checklist, Ines, the help desk technician, disables Dev's account that afternoon, ends its sessions and revokes the access token on Dev's phone app for the shipping portal. Customers still email Dev, so Ines asks the sales director, who owns the customer records, which colleague should receive the mailbox.

review: Confirm every exit checklist step is done and recorded
Confirm shared passwords the leaver knew were changed
evidence: Leaver report matched to disabled accounts and the time disabled
Accounts still active after their HR end date
audit_focus.recommend: Report any leaver account still active after the end date to the system owner at once.
audit_focus.decides: HR sets the end date; the data owner decides on the data

subtopics.isaca_rule: Remove access as fast as the risk demands: the same day as a rule, and as the person is told for a hostile exit.

exam_traps.trap: Delete the leaver's account immediately to be safe.
exam_traps.why: Deleting can lose data and break the link between logs and the person. Disable now, delete later.

exam_traps.trap: Disabling the main account removes all access.
exam_traps.why: Sessions, access keys, remote access and shared passwords can survive. Revoke each one.

key_terms.definition: An exit where the person may cause harm, so access is cut as they are told.
Ending a user's active sign-ins so open sessions stop working at once.

subtopics.name: Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle
subtopics.definition: Non-human identities are accounts used by software, such as service accounts, bots, application programming interface (API) keys and AI agents. They need the same life cycle as people.
subtopics.why_it_matters: They often outnumber staff and never resign. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) ranks improper offboarding and leaked secrets as their top risks.
how_it_works: Give each one a named human owner, a purpose and an inventory entry.
Give each workload or agent its own identity, never a borrowed staff login.
Keep secrets in a vault, not in code or chat; owners rotate them on schedule and after exposure.
Deleting a leaked secret from chat or code does not revoke it; anyone who copied it can use it until it is rotated.
Retire the identity when its owner leaves or the project ends, unless a new owner takes it on.
subtopics.example: A ferry operator replaced its AI timetable-planning agent with a vendor's tool in March, but in June the old agent's account and access token still work. Elif, a junior cloud engineer, spots them in the monthly identity inventory and asks the owner listed for the agent if anything depends on them. Once the owner confirms nothing does, Elif disables the account, revokes the token and updates the inventory.

review: Confirm each service account, key and agent has an owner
Check code, tickets and chat for exposed secrets
evidence: Secret-scanning results for code repositories
Keys and service accounts with no owner or recent use
audit_focus.recommend: Report exposed keys and ownerless service accounts to the security team for rotation or removal.
audit_focus.decides: The named owner decides whether the identity is still needed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat every bot, key and agent like a badged worker: an owner, a purpose, least access and an end date.

exam_traps.trap: Service accounts need no review because nobody signs in with them.
exam_traps.why: They often hold broad, long-lived access that attackers target. Review them with their owner.

exam_traps.trap: An AI agent can safely use a staff member's own login.
exam_traps.why: It then gets all the person's rights and its actions look like theirs. Give it its own identity.

key_terms.definition: A secret string a program presents to prove which application is calling.
Software that uses an AI model to plan and take actions, such as calling tools, for someone.

subtopics.name: IAM Frameworks and Tools
subtopics.definition: Identity and access management (IAM) frameworks are published guides to good identity practice; IAM tools are the systems that carry it out, such as directories and governance platforms.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Frameworks give a shared, defensible standard instead of one person's opinion. Tools make the life cycle repeatable and keep the records reviews need.
how_it_works: Frameworks set out good practice, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) identity guidelines.
Other control catalogs, listed in the references, add practical steps for accounts and access.
Zero Trust checks identity and context on every request, not network location (see 4.2.6).
Tools connect: human resources feeds identity governance, which creates directory accounts.

types.meaning: The central store of users, groups and their attributes that systems look up
Runs requests, approvals, provisioning and access reviews, and keeps the records
Guards administrator accounts with a vault, time-limited access and session logs

subtopics.example: A 40-person accounting firm tracks access in a spreadsheet, and two leavers kept email for weeks. Noor, the new IT associate, maps the firm's steps against a recognized framework's account controls, lists the gaps and suggests linking the human resources system to the cloud directory. Noor presents the list for the office manager to decide.

review: Map current IAM steps against one framework to find gaps
Confirm each access change has a record in the tool
evidence: Recent starts and exits matched to changes in the directory
Connector logs showing human resources changes reaching the directory
audit_focus.recommend: Present gaps and tool options to your manager; leadership chooses frameworks and spending.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses the framework, tools and IAM budget

subtopics.isaca_rule: Frameworks say what good looks like; tools make it repeatable, driven by a trusted source and kept on record.

exam_traps.trap: Buying an IAM tool solves access problems by itself.
exam_traps.why: A tool automates whatever process it is given. Without roles, owners and reviews, it automates the mess.

exam_traps.trap: A request from inside the office network can be trusted.
exam_traps.why: Zero Trust checks identity and context on every request; location alone proves nothing.

key_terms.definition: How confident a system can be in a sign-in; NIST defines levels 1 to 3, with 3 the strongest.
A published, usually voluntary set of practices for organizing security work, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) CSF 2.0.

subtopics.name: Access Requests and Approvals
subtopics.definition: An access request is a recorded ask for a specific right. The owner of the resource approves it, and a different person fulfills and records it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most access changes happen after day one. A request path stops rights being granted on a hallway word or a convincing message, and leaves a record.
how_it_works: The requester names the exact access, the reason and how long it is needed.
The resource or data owner approves; nobody approves their own request.
The person who grants the access is not the person who approved it.
Urgent or unusual requests are verified through a known channel first.
subtopics.example: At a seed supplier, a ticket asks for edit rights on the price list for Femi, a field rep. It shows as approved, but the approver is Femi's teammate, not the pricing manager who owns the list. Jules, a help desk analyst, holds the ticket, sends it to the pricing manager for approval and grants the access only once that approval is recorded.

review: Match each grant to an approved request
Look for self-approved requests or approvers who also fulfilled
evidence: Request tickets showing requester, approver, fulfiller and end date
Directory changes made with no matching ticket
audit_focus.recommend: Send requests lacking approval, or pushing to skip it, back to the resource owner.
audit_focus.decides: Resource owners decide; the help desk only fulfills approved requests

subtopics.isaca_rule: No ticket, no access. The owner approves, someone else fulfills, and the record shows both. Urgency changes how fast a request moves, never whether it is checked.

exam_traps.trap: An approval forwarded by email from a senior manager is enough.
exam_traps.why: Email is easy to fake. Use the request system, and confirm unusual requests through a known channel.

exam_traps.trap: The help desk can approve the access it grants, since it knows the systems.
exam_traps.why: Knowing a system is not owning its data. The owner approves; the help desk fulfills.

key_terms.definition: Carrying out an approved request in the systems, done by someone other than the approver.
Confirming a request through a separate, trusted channel already on file, such as a known phone number (a callback), never one given in the request.

subtopics.name: Third-Party, Guest and Federated Access
subtopics.definition: Third-party access lets contractors, vendors and partners use your systems, through guest accounts you create or by trusting their own organization's sign-in through federation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Outside users are often forgotten when their work ends, and their employer may never tell you they left.
how_it_works: Each outside user has an internal sponsor who requests the access and answers for it.
Access is time-limited, matched to the contract and included in access reviews.
With federation, the partner proves who the user is; your owner still decides what they may do.
Contracts should require partners to report staff who leave or change roles.
subtopics.example: A city water utility gives an engineering firm's staff guest accounts on its project site. Nadia, an access analyst, ties each account's expiry to the contract and names the utility's project manager to answer for it. When the firm asks to keep one engineer's access for a follow-up visit, Nadia extends it only after the project manager, as sponsor, approves.

review: Confirm every guest or vendor account has a sponsor and end date
Compare the guest list with the partner's current staff list
evidence: Guest account report with sponsor, last sign-in and expiry
Contract clauses on leaver notice and permitted access
audit_focus.recommend: Report outside accounts with no sponsor, or past their end date, to the vendor manager.
audit_focus.decides: The sponsor and resource owner decide what outsiders may reach

subtopics.isaca_rule: Federation shares proof of identity, not permission. The partner vouches for who someone is; your owner decides what they may reach and for how long.

exam_traps.trap: Once we trust a partner's sign-in, the partner decides what its staff can reach.
exam_traps.why: Federation only passes on who the user is. Your resource owner still authorizes, limits and removes access.

exam_traps.trap: Guest accounts need no review because the people work elsewhere.
exam_traps.why: The risk sits on your systems. Give guests sponsors and end dates, and review them.

key_terms.definition: The internal person who requests an outside user's access and confirms it is still needed.
Trust between organizations, set by agreement and exchanged keys, that lets one accept the other's sign-ins.

subtopics.name: Sessions, Timeouts and Reauthentication
subtopics.definition: A session is the period after sign-in when a user can act without proving their identity again. Session controls decide how long it lasts and when to check again.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A stolen session token or an unlocked screen gives someone the user's access without any password. Session limits shrink that window.
how_it_works: An inactivity timeout ends or locks a session after a period with no activity.
An overall timeout ends a session after a set time, however active the user is.
At its highest assurance level, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) caps sessions at 12 hours and recommends a 15-minute idle limit.
Ask users to sign in again before sensitive actions, such as changing bank details.
subtopics.example: At an insurance call center, a test shows that claims portal sessions stay valid until the next morning, even after staff sign out or close the browser at the end of a shift. Bea, a junior security analyst, writes up the gap, suggests that signing out end the session on the server and that sessions expire after a shift's length, and raises a change request for the system owner to approve.

review: Compare each system's idle and overall timeouts with the standard
Confirm signing out ends the session on every device
evidence: Session timeout settings for each key application
Logs of sessions that stayed open far beyond the limit
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the system owner to fix any timeout weaker than the standard, through change control.
audit_focus.decides: The security manager sets timeout values; system owners apply them

subtopics.isaca_rule: Proving identity once is not enough forever: match session limits to the risk and check again before risky actions.

exam_traps.trap: After a strong sign-in, a session can safely stay open all day.
exam_traps.why: Strong sign-in protects the start, not the hours after. A stolen token or unlocked screen skips it.

exam_traps.trap: Closing the browser tab always signs the user out.
exam_traps.why: Many sessions stay valid until they time out or are revoked. Sign out properly.

key_terms.definition: A value issued after sign-in that proves the session; anyone who steals it can act as the user.
Asking a signed-in user to prove their identity again, after a timeout or before a sensitive action.

topics.overview: Logical access controls are the software rules that decide what a signed-in identity may read, change or run. This topic covers the principles that set the limits (least privilege, need to know and separation of duties), the extra care privileged and automated accounts need, and the access control models, which differ in who sets the rules: the owner, the system, roles, attributes or fixed rules.
can_do: Apply least privilege and need to know to choose the smallest access that still lets the work get done
Spot a separation of duties conflict and name a fitting fix or compensating control
Name the access control model (DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC or rule-based) from who decides in a short scenario
Limit privileged, service and AI agent access with just-in-time grants, approval and logging

subtopics.name: Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions
subtopics.definition: Logical access controls are software rules that decide whether a subject, such as a user or process, may perform an action on an object, such as a file.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Once someone is signed in, these rules stop them reading payroll or deleting records they should not touch.
how_it_works: A subject (a user, process or AI agent) asks to read, write, run or delete an object.
The system checks the object's permissions; anything not explicitly allowed is refused.
Grant permissions to groups or roles, not individuals, so changes and reviews stay manageable.
Accounting, the third A of authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA), records each access decision so misuse can be traced; it grants or blocks nothing.
subtopics.example: At a small law firm, a paralegal can open every client folder because the folders were shared with Everyone years ago. Sol, the IT assistant, notices while setting up a new folder, lists the open folders and asks the managing partner, who owns the client files, which teams should keep access to each.

review: Look for permissions granted to individuals instead of groups
Look for Everyone or all-users permissions on sensitive data
evidence: Permission reports for folders that hold sensitive data
Logs of permission changes and denied access attempts
audit_focus.recommend: Report over-broad permissions on sensitive data to the data owner and the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner sets which teams may open their files

subtopics.isaca_rule: Authentication says who you are; logical access controls say what you can touch. Start from default deny and grant through groups.

exam_traps.trap: Once users are authenticated, they can open anything on the network.
exam_traps.why: Authentication only proves identity. Authorization still limits each identity to what its job needs.

key_terms.definition: The active party asking for access, such as a user, process or AI agent.
The resource being accessed, such as a file, database or application.
A list on an object naming who may access it and how; network access lists (see 4.1.7) filter traffic instead.
The rule that any access not explicitly allowed is refused; also called implicit deny.
The third A of AAA: recording what each identity did, so actions can be traced. It grants or blocks nothing (see 1.1.6).

subtopics.name: Least Privilege and Need to Know
subtopics.definition: Least privilege gives each user or process the minimum access its task needs, for as long as needed. Need to know limits information to people whose duties require it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If an account is stolen or misused, least privilege limits the damage to what it could reach. Nobody can delete what they cannot touch.
how_it_works: Start with no access and add only what the task requires.
Keep everyday and admin accounts separate, so email never runs with admin rights.
Add time limits, so temporary access ends when the task does.
Need to know is a second test: someone cleared for sensitive data sees only their own cases.

rows.label: What it limits
cells: The actions a subject can perform
The information a person can see

rows.label: Question it asks
cells: What is the least this task can run with?
Does this person's current work require this data?

rows.label: Example
cells: A help desk agent can reset passwords but not change admin groups
A nurse sees records for patients in their care, not every patient

subtopics.example: A fitness club chain's member app shows front-desk staff each member's health notes, which only trainers need. Sasha, the IT coordinator, confirms the desk needs only names and membership status to check members in, then asks the operations manager, who owns member data, to approve hiding the health-notes field from the desk role.

review: Compare requested rights with what the task actually does
Confirm administrators use a separate account for admin work
evidence: Accounts with admin rights compared with their job needs
Temporary grants that are past their end date
audit_focus.recommend: Raise requests for broad or permanent rights with the data owner instead of approving them yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner approves access beyond the standard role

subtopics.isaca_rule: Give the smallest access that lets the work happen, with an end date. Convenience and seniority are not reasons for more.

exam_traps.trap: Senior managers should get broad access because of their position.
exam_traps.why: Rank is not a task. Senior accounts are prime targets and need least privilege too.

exam_traps.trap: A clearance for a level means seeing all data at that level.
exam_traps.why: Clearance is only the first test. Need to know limits a cleared person to the data their work requires.

key_terms.definition: Gaining more rights than granted through a flaw; least privilege limits what an attacker starts with.
Rights held all the time, whether or not in use; the opposite of time-limited access.

subtopics.memory_aid: Least privilege limits what you can do; need to know limits what you can see.

subtopics.name: Separation of Duties and Two-Person Control
subtopics.definition: Separation of duties (SoD) splits a sensitive task so no single person can complete it alone; two-person control requires two people to act together.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One person with end-to-end control can commit and hide fraud or a costly mistake. Splitting duties means abuse needs collusion.
how_it_works: Separate who requests, approves, carries out and checks a sensitive task.
Classic conflicts: adding a supplier and paying it, or writing code and releasing it.
An approval counts only if an approved item cannot be changed without a fresh approval.
Check new roles and access requests for conflicts before granting them.
A second account for the same person splits nothing; separation of duties needs a second person.
Teams too small to split duties use compensating controls, such as independent review.

types.meaning: Two people must each act to finish a task, such as two approvals for a large transfer
Two authorized people must be present and act together, such as at a critical key ceremony
Each person holds only part of a secret, so nobody knows all of it

subtopics.example: At a payment processor, the passphrase that unlocks the card system's master key is split between two key holders, each keeping half in a separate safe. Lucia, one holder, is moving to the marketing team, and the operations manager suggests handing Lucia's half to the other holder. Farah, a junior security analyst, points out that one person would then know the whole secret and asks the system owner to appoint a new holder and have the passphrase changed.

review: Compare each person's rights against a list of conflicting duties
Look for small-team conflicts with no compensating control
evidence: SoD conflict report from the access or finance system
Sign-off records for independent reviews of high-risk transactions
audit_focus.recommend: Report SoD conflicts to the system owner; never quietly give one person both duties.
audit_focus.decides: The policy owner approves a compensating control as an exception; the risk owner accepts what remains

subtopics.isaca_rule: No one person should be able to start, approve and hide a sensitive action. Split duties, or add independent review.

exam_traps.trap: Separation of duties and least privilege are the same thing.
exam_traps.why: Least privilege limits how much one person can do; SoD splits a process across people. Minimal rights can still conflict.

exam_traps.trap: A trusted, long-serving employee can hold conflicting duties.
exam_traps.why: SoD is not about distrust. It protects the organization, and the employee, from fraud and suspicion.

key_terms.definition: People secretly working together to get around a control such as separation of duties.
An alternative control that lowers the same risk when the usual one, such as patching, is not possible; approved as a recorded exception.
Moving a duty between trained people from time to time, so hidden errors or misuse surface; it does not stop one harmful act.

subtopics.name: Privileged Access Management
subtopics.definition: Privileged access management (PAM) controls accounts that can change systems, security settings or other users' access, such as administrator, root and database owner accounts.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Privileged accounts are the keys attackers want most: one compromise can switch off defenses or reach everything.
how_it_works: Inventory every privileged account, including built-in, service and cloud console accounts.
Each administrator uses a named admin account for admin work only, never a shared one.
A vault checks admin credentials out, rotates them and logs each use.
Require phishing-resistant sign-in, record privileged sessions and grant rights just in time (see 3.2.12).
subtopics.example: At a manufacturing plant, five engineers have shared one admin password for three years. When an overnight change stops the line, nobody can tell who made it. Fatima, a junior security analyst, records the gap in the risk log and drafts a proposal for named admin accounts and a vault for the system owner.

review: Confirm every admin or root account is inventoried, built-in ones too
Look for admin accounts used for email or web browsing
evidence: Change tickets matched to each privileged sign-in
Privileged accounts without strong sign-in or outside the vault
audit_focus.recommend: Raise shared or unvaulted privileged credentials with the security team for tracking.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner approves who holds privileged access, and how long

subtopics.isaca_rule: The more power an account has, the tighter its controls: named accounts, strong sign-in, a vault, time limits and recorded sessions.

exam_traps.trap: Administrators can read email with their admin account to save time.
exam_traps.why: Email and browsing are where phishing and malicious software arrive. With admin rights, one click gives an attacker full control.

exam_traps.trap: Sharing one admin password is fine if only trusted engineers know it.
exam_traps.why: A shared account cannot show who acted. Use named admin accounts through a vault.

key_terms.definition: Capturing what an administrator does in a privileged session, so it can be reviewed later.
A default administrator account that ships with a system or device, often with a known name.

subtopics.name: Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
subtopics.definition: Discretionary access control (DAC) lets the owner of a resource, usually its creator, decide who else may access it and what they may do.
subtopics.why_it_matters: DAC is how most file shares and cloud documents work: flexible, but data can be overshared with one click.
how_it_works: The owner sets permissions on their own files, often through an access control list.
People the owner shares with may be able to share again.
Weaknesses: oversharing, and malware (malicious software) running with the user's rights.
Organizations limit DAC with sharing restrictions, labels and access reviews.
subtopics.example: Robin, a design studio's project lead, shares a contract folder with a freelancer through an anyone-with-the-link setting, and the link turns up on a public forum. Ezra, the IT assistant, gets the alert and follows the incident procedure: switch the folder to named people, then report the exposure to the studio manager.

review: Confirm each shared sensitive folder has a recorded owner
Look for open link sharing on folders that hold sensitive data
evidence: Sharing reports listing files shared externally or by link
The owner recorded for each shared folder
audit_focus.recommend: Report sensitive data shared outside the organization to the data owner, following the incident procedure.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides who may see the data, within policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: In DAC the owner decides: flexible, but add sharing limits and reviews when the data is sensitive.

exam_traps.trap: Under DAC, a central administrator decides who gets access.
exam_traps.why: Central decisions describe non-discretionary models such as role-based control. In DAC the owner decides.

exam_traps.trap: DAC is the most secure model because owners know their data.
exam_traps.why: Owners overshare by mistake, and malware inherits their rights. DAC is the most flexible model, not the strictest.

key_terms.definition: The person who owns a file or object and, under DAC, controls who can use it.
Access for anyone holding a file's web link; convenient but easy to forward.

subtopics.memory_aid: DAC: the owner's Discretion. Mandatory control (MAC): the system's Mandate.

subtopics.name: Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
subtopics.definition: Mandatory access control (MAC) lets the system, not the owner, decide access by comparing a subject's clearance with the object's classification label under central policy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: MAC protects data that one user's choice must never leak, as in military systems. It is not the network MAC address (Domain 4).
how_it_works: Every object carries a security label, such as Confidential or Secret.
Every subject has a clearance, set by a central security authority.
Access needs enough clearance plus a need to know; users cannot change labels, even on their own files.
MAC is strong but rigid and costly, so it suits high-security settings.
subtopics.example: At a navy shipyard, a test manager adds Kofi, a contractor cleared only to Confidential, to the manager's own folder of Secret trial results so Kofi can help write them up. The system still turns Kofi away: under MAC, an owner's sharing cannot outweigh the label. Kofi calls the help desk. Ruth, the help desk analyst, leaves labels and rights alone, logs the ticket as working as designed and reports the attempted share to the security officer.

review: Confirm new data carries the correct classification label
Confirm data moved to a lower level has an approved release
evidence: Denied access events showing label and clearance mismatches
Records of who changed labels or clearances, and who approved
audit_focus.recommend: Report attempts to bypass labels or clearances to the security officer straight away.
audit_focus.decides: The central security officer sets labels, clearances and releases

subtopics.isaca_rule: In MAC the system enforces labels and clearances, and nobody, not even the creator, can override them.

exam_traps.trap: The creator of a file can share it under MAC because they own it.
exam_traps.why: Ownership gives no control in MAC. Centrally set labels and clearances decide.

exam_traps.trap: A Top Secret clearance opens every Top Secret file.
exam_traps.why: MAC also checks need to know, often through compartments. Clearance is necessary but not enough.

key_terms.definition: A classification marking, such as Secret, that the system reads to decide access.
The highest classification level a person is approved to access, granted after vetting.
A named category within a level, such as a project, that adds a need-to-know check.

subtopics.name: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
subtopics.definition: Role-based access control (RBAC) attaches permissions to roles that match job functions, then assigns people to roles, so access follows the job rather than the person.
subtopics.why_it_matters: RBAC is the most common model in business systems because it scales. Changing someone's job means changing their role.
how_it_works: Permissions attach to roles, such as Nurse or Billing clerk, and people are assigned roles.
A person's roles add together, which can create conflicts.
Movers change roles and leavers lose all roles, so the life cycle maps neatly onto RBAC.
RBAC weakens when custom roles multiply or rights are granted outside any role.
subtopics.example: A clinic's records system grants access by role. When Elena, a receptionist, qualifies as a medical assistant, the practice manager approves the change. Hana, the IT coordinator, swaps Elena's Receptionist role for Medical Assistant, so access changes in minutes, then confirms no one-off permissions remain from the old job.

review: Look for access copied from another user instead of a role
Compare each person's combined roles with the conflict list
evidence: Membership lists for each sensitive role
Direct grants that bypass the role catalog
audit_focus.recommend: Report one-off permissions or conflicting roles to the role owner for a decision.
audit_focus.decides: The role owner, usually the business or data owner, approves contents and membership

subtopics.isaca_rule: When access follows the job, think RBAC. It is non-discretionary: the organization defines roles, and users cannot hand out rights.

exam_traps.trap: RBAC lets each user decide who joins their role.
exam_traps.why: The organization sets role membership through an approved process. That is what makes RBAC non-discretionary.

exam_traps.trap: RBAC alone can block access by time of day or location.
exam_traps.why: Plain RBAC checks only the role. Time or location needs rules or attributes.

key_terms.definition: A named set of permissions that matches a job function, such as Accounts Clerk.
Roles policy forbids one person to hold together, such as Requester and Approver.

subtopics.name: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
subtopics.definition: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) decides each request by checking a policy against attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the environment, such as time or location.
subtopics.why_it_matters: ABAC handles fine-grained, changing conditions that roles cannot, such as approving expenses only for one's own region, in business hours, from a managed device.
how_it_works: Subject attributes describe the user, such as department or training completed.
Object attributes describe the resource; environment attributes describe the moment, such as time or device health.
A policy engine checks each request, so access changes as attributes change, without new roles.
Decisions are only as good as the attributes: one wrong value changes the answer.
subtopics.example: An international charity's grant files must be readable only by staff in the same country office, on managed laptops; a role for every country and device would mean hundreds. Omar, a junior cloud administrator, helps build an ABAC policy on the user's country, the file's country tag and device status, and tests it before release.

review: Test each policy with sample users before it goes live
Compare key attributes with their source, such as human resources records
evidence: Policy test results for both allowed and denied cases
Attribute source records, such as the department field
audit_focus.recommend: Report a policy that grants unexpected access to the policy owner before it is used.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner and the security team approve the access policies

subtopics.isaca_rule: Several conditions at once, such as who, where and when: think ABAC. Wrong attributes mean wrong decisions.

exam_traps.trap: ABAC is just role-based control with more roles.
exam_traps.why: ABAC needs no role per case. It checks attributes on every request, so one policy covers many combinations.

exam_traps.trap: A correctly written ABAC policy cannot grant the wrong access.
exam_traps.why: ABAC trusts its attributes. A stale department field in the human resources system can grant or block wrongly.

key_terms.definition: A characteristic used in an access decision, such as department, data label, location or time.
The component that checks each request against the access policy and returns allow or deny.

subtopics.name: Rule-Based Access Control
subtopics.definition: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules, set by an administrator, to every subject alike, such as firewall rules or a ban on sign-ins outside business hours.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Rules set limits whoever the user is, which suits network traffic, hours and locations. Do not confuse it with role-based access control (RBAC).
how_it_works: An administrator writes the rules; the system applies them to every matching request.
Rules are checked in order, the first match decides, and a final rule denies the rest.
Typical uses: firewall rules, time-of-day limits and blocked countries.
Rules often sit on top of roles: the role sets what a nurse can do; a rule limits where.
An exception the rule's owner approves covers only the person, place and period that need it, then expires.
subtopics.example: A payroll system is used only in office hours, yet its logs show 3 a.m. sign-in attempts. Avery, a junior network administrator, raises a change request and, once it is approved, adds a rule blocking payroll sign-ins from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m., except for the on-call group, then checks the logs to confirm it works.

review: Match recent rule changes to approved change tickets
Confirm the last rule denies anything not already allowed
evidence: Rule list showing an owner and purpose for each rule
Hit counts showing which rules are used and which never match
audit_focus.recommend: Report rules nobody can explain to the rule owner instead of deleting them yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The network or system owner approves each rule and its removal

subtopics.isaca_rule: The same administrator rule for everyone: think rule-based. Access that depends on the person's job: think role-based.

exam_traps.trap: Rule-based and role-based access control are the same model.
exam_traps.why: Role-based ties rights to jobs. Rule-based applies the same conditions, such as time or address, to everyone.

exam_traps.trap: Rules can be added freely, since each allows only a little.
exam_traps.why: Rules pile up and interact. Each needs an owner, a purpose and periodic review.

key_terms.definition: A final rule that blocks anything earlier rules did not allow, putting default deny into practice.
Any model where central policy, not the owner, decides: mandatory, role-based, attribute-based or rule-based.

subtopics.name: Choosing an Access Control Model
subtopics.definition: Choosing an access control model starts with one question: who or what decides access (the owner, labels, job roles, attributes or fixed rules), and does that fit the risk?
subtopics.why_it_matters: Scenarios describe who decides rather than naming the model, and real organizations mix models, so knowing where each fits avoids a poor choice.
how_it_works: Ask who decides: the owner means discretionary (DAC); central labels, mandatory (MAC); job roles, role-based (RBAC).
Ask what it depends on: many conditions mean attribute-based (ABAC); one fixed rule for all, rule-based.
Most businesses use RBAC; classified data suits MAC; personal folders suit DAC.
Combine models where it helps, such as RBAC for applications and rules on the firewall.

rows.label: DAC
cells: The resource owner
Small teams, personal and shared files
Oversharing; malware gets the user's rights

rows.label: MAC
cells: The system, using labels and clearances
Classified or highly sensitive data
Rigid and costly to run

rows.label: RBAC
cells: The organization, through job roles
Most business applications
Role explosion and copied access

rows.label: ABAC
cells: A policy over many attributes
Fine-grained, changing conditions
Complexity; depends on accurate attributes

rows.label: Rule-based
cells: Administrator rules, the same for all
Firewalls, time and location limits
Rule sprawl; confusion with role-based

subtopics.example: A veterinary chain of 12 clinics gives each new hire whatever their predecessor had. Avi, a junior IT analyst, notices that staff fall into five job types and suggests RBAC, plus a rule blocking sign-ins to the drug inventory outside clinic hours. Avi presents both options, with the risks each reduces, to the operations director.

review: Identify who decides, and on what, before naming a model
Confirm each major system's access follows its chosen model
evidence: Each system's access settings showing owner, role or rule decisions
Exceptions where users hold access outside the chosen model
audit_focus.recommend: Bring proposals to change a system's model to the system owner and the security team.
audit_focus.decides: Management and system owners choose the model, based on risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Read the scenario for the decider, then choose the model that fits the risk, not simply the strictest one.

exam_traps.trap: Pick MAC every time, because the strictest model is the most secure.
exam_traps.why: MAC is rigid and costly. The best model fits the data and the organization; most businesses use RBAC.

exam_traps.trap: An organization must use one model for everything.
exam_traps.why: Mixing is normal: roles for applications, owner sharing for personal folders, rules on network devices.

key_terms.definition: A formal approach setting who or what decides access.
Using more than one access control model in one organization, each where it fits best.

subtopics.name: Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents
subtopics.definition: Applying least privilege and separation of duties to automation means scripts, bots and AI agents get only the access their task needs and cannot finish high-risk actions alone.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An over-privileged bot or a manipulated AI agent can do damage in seconds. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) calls this risk excessive agency.
how_it_works: Scope each bot or agent to the data, tools and actions its task needs, never beyond its user's rights.
Keep a human approval step for high-impact actions, such as payments or deletions.
One automation should not both make a change and approve it.
Log actions under the agent's own identity, keep a stop switch and treat instructions in content as untrusted.
subtopics.example: A travel booking firm's build bot uses a token that can change every code repository, though it only builds the mobile app. Tobi, a junior developer, lists what the bot actually does and proposes to the system owner a token limited to that app's repository, with a person approving each release to customers.

review: Look for agent permissions that no documented task uses
Test that the agent stops and waits at each approval step
evidence: The agent's permission list compared with its documented tasks
Activity logs that tie each action to a specific agent
audit_focus.recommend: Report an agent or bot with broad or unexplained rights to its owner and the security team.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides what automation may do unattended

subtopics.isaca_rule: Automation follows people's rules, more strictly: its own identity, least privilege, human approval for risky actions, logs and a stop switch.

exam_traps.trap: An AI agent is just software, so access principles do not apply to it.
exam_traps.why: An agent reads data and takes actions like a user. It needs its own identity, scoped rights and oversight.

exam_traps.trap: Broad access for an AI agent is safe when the vendor is reputable.
exam_traps.why: A manipulated or faulty agent can misuse broad access whoever made it. Grant per task.

key_terms.definition: An AI system given more permissions or independence than its task needs.
Crafted or hidden instructions in input or content that try to make an AI tool ignore its original instructions or rules.

subtopics.name: Just-in-Time and Break-Glass Access
subtopics.definition: Just-in-time access grants privileged rights only for an approved task and period, then removes them. Break-glass access is a sealed emergency account for when normal access fails.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Standing admin rights are available to attackers around the clock. Granting them only when needed shrinks that window.
how_it_works: An administrator requests elevation for a named task, and an approver agrees.
The rights switch on for a set time, the session is logged, and the rights expire.
Break-glass credentials are sealed in a vault or safe, held by few people and tested regularly.
Keep break-glass sign-in independent of the normal path, such as single sign-on (SSO), so it works when that path fails.
Every break-glass use raises an alert and a review, and the credential is changed afterward.
subtopics.example: On a quiet Sunday, a regional airport's monitoring raises an alert: the baggage system's break-glass account was opened while normal sign-in was working. Rosa, a junior security analyst, checks the emergency log, finds no recorded incident and, as the runbook directs, reports the use to the incident response lead as a possible incident. The system owner then has the account's password changed.

review: Confirm each elevation had an approved task and expired on time
Match every emergency sign-in to an incident record
evidence: Elevation logs with requester, approver, start and end times
Alerts and session records for each emergency account use
audit_focus.recommend: Report break-glass use with no incident record, or elevation that never expired, to the system owner.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner approves who may elevate or hold emergency access

subtopics.isaca_rule: Privilege should be borrowed, not owned: request it for a task, use it, let it expire. Emergency access must exist, but every use is alerted and reviewed.

exam_traps.trap: Give administrators permanent admin rights so they can respond quickly.
exam_traps.why: Standing rights help attackers too. Just-in-time grants and a tested break-glass account give speed without permanent exposure.

exam_traps.trap: A break-glass account can go unmonitored, since it is only for emergencies.
exam_traps.why: Its power and rare use make every sign-in worth checking.

key_terms.definition: Privileged rights granted only for an approved task and period, then removed automatically.
A sealed emergency account for when normal admin access fails; every use raises an alert.

subtopics.name: Access Model Scenarios: Worked Examples
subtopics.definition: Worked scenarios practice naming the access control model from clues: who sets the permission, what the decision depends on, and whether users can change it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Short scenarios describe the decision instead of naming the model. Reading for the decider, not for words like secure or flexible, settles most choices.
how_it_works: Find the decider: an owner, a central label, a job role, attributes or one rule for all.
If users cannot change access themselves, such as when access is set centrally or sharing is blocked, the model is non-discretionary.
Groups do not always mean role-based: if a file owner picks the group, it is discretionary.
A time limit applied to everyone is rule-based, even where roles also exist.

rows.label: Case 1
cells: A manager shares a budget sheet with two colleagues
The file's owner
Discretionary (DAC)

rows.label: Case 2
cells: Only staff cleared to Secret, on that project, can open a design
The system, by label and clearance
Mandatory (MAC)

rows.label: Case 3
cells: New pharmacists get the Pharmacist permissions on day one
The organization, by job role
Role-based (RBAC)

rows.label: Case 4
cells: Managers approve expenses for their own region, on work laptops, in office hours
A policy over several attributes
Attribute-based (ABAC)

rows.label: Case 5
cells: Nobody can sign in to payroll between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m.
One administrator rule for all
Rule-based

subtopics.example: Imani, a new access analyst at a research lab, documents two systems. Anyone in the Technician role can book lab equipment, while the results database opens only to staff whose training record shows a current data-handling course and who connect from a lab-managed device, checked at each request. Imani first writes role-based for both, then splits them: the job role decides equipment booking, and the training and device attributes decide the database.

review: Compare a few real permission grants with the recorded model
Look for systems with no access model recorded
evidence: Permission settings showing whether owners, roles or rules grant access
Model inventory listing each application and its access model
audit_focus.recommend: Flag systems whose recorded model differs from their real settings to the system owner.
audit_focus.decides: System owners confirm which model their system uses

subtopics.isaca_rule: When two models seem to fit, split the scenario into parts and name the model for each part.

exam_traps.trap: If permissions go to groups, the model must be role-based.
exam_traps.why: Owners share with groups too. If the file owner chose the group, it is discretionary.

exam_traps.trap: Any scenario with classified data uses mandatory access control.
exam_traps.why: Check who decides. If the owner can grant access at will, it is discretionary, whatever the label says.

key_terms.definition: A named set of accounts given the same permissions; whether the resource owner or central policy picks its members points to the access control model.
A limit that blocks access outside set hours. One hours rule for everyone points to rule-based; hours weighed with other attributes point to ABAC.

key_terminologies.Identity: The record that represents one person or system across the organization.
key_terminologies.Identification: Claiming an identity, such as by entering a username; it proves nothing until authentication verifies it.
key_terminologies.Authentication: Proving a claimed identity with one or more factors.
key_terminologies.Authorization: Deciding what an authenticated identity may do.
key_terminologies.Identity life cycle: The joiner, mover and leaver stages an identity passes through, with reviews alongside (also written lifecycle).
key_terminologies.Provisioning: Creating an account and granting its approved access.
key_terminologies.Deprovisioning: Removing an identity's access, credentials and sessions when they are no longer needed.
key_terminologies.Access review: A regular check by a manager or owner that each account and right is still needed.
key_terminologies.Privilege creep: The buildup of unneeded access as people change jobs and keep old rights.
key_terminologies.Access request: A recorded ask for specific access, approved by the resource owner and fulfilled by someone else.
key_terminologies.Multifactor authentication (MFA): Sign-in that combines at least two different factor categories: something you know, something you have or something you are.
key_terminologies.Phishing-resistant authentication: Sign-in tied to the genuine site, such as passkeys and Fast Identity Online 2 (FIDO2) keys, that a fake page cannot capture and reuse.
key_terminologies.Single sign-on (SSO): One sign-in at an identity provider that gives access to many applications.
key_terminologies.Federation: Trust between organizations, set by agreement and exchanged keys, that lets one accept the other's sign-ins.
key_terminologies.Adaptive authentication: Sign-in checks that rise or fall with the risk score of each attempt.
key_terminologies.Session: The period after sign-in when a user can act without proving identity again; timeouts limit it.
key_terminologies.Least privilege: Giving each identity only the access its task needs, for only as long as needed.
key_terminologies.Need to know: Limiting information to people whose current duties require it, even if their clearance would allow more.
key_terminologies.Separation of duties (SoD): Splitting a sensitive process so no single person can complete it alone.
key_terminologies.Privileged account: An account that can change systems, security settings or other users' access, so misuse can do serious harm.
key_terminologies.Privileged access management (PAM): Tools and practices that vault admin credentials, grant them just in time and record privileged sessions.
key_terminologies.Just-in-time (JIT) access: Privileged rights granted only for an approved task and period, then removed automatically.
key_terminologies.Service account: A non-human account used by an application, process or AI agent rather than a person.
key_terminologies.Non-human identity: Any identity used by software, such as a service account, bot, application programming interface (API) key or AI agent.
key_terminologies.Discretionary access control (DAC): The resource owner decides who may access it.
key_terminologies.Mandatory access control (MAC): The system decides access by comparing clearances with classification labels; not the same as a network MAC address.
key_terminologies.Role-based access control (RBAC): Permissions attach to job roles, and people are assigned roles.
key_terminologies.Attribute-based access control (ABAC): A policy decides each request using attributes of the user, resource, action and environment.
key_terminologies.Rule-based access control: Administrator-written rules apply the same way to every subject.
